background.title: Atoms, electrons and covalent bonds
background.html:
Everything is made of tiny atoms. Each atom has a small centre with electrons (tiny negative particles) around it. The electrons in the outermost layer, the outer shell, take part in bonding.

In a covalent bond two atoms share a pair of electrons. It is strong. A single bond (C-C) shares one pair; a double bond (C=C) shares two pairs.

Each kind of atom makes a fixed number of covalent bonds: hydrogen 1, oxygen 2, nitrogen 3, carbon 4. A double bond counts as two of them.

background.title: Reading a formula and counting atoms
background.html:
A formula lists the atoms in one molecule. The small low number after a symbol counts that atom: C6H12O6 (glucose) has 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 6 oxygen atoms. H2O (water) has 2 hydrogen and 1 oxygen.

Groups of atoms have short names: -OH is an oxygen joined to a hydrogen (a hydroxyl group); -COOH is an acid group; CH2OH is a carbon with two hydrogens and an -OH.

In ring diagrams, the corners of the ring are atoms (usually carbon), and the lines are covalent bonds.

background.title: Polar, non-polar and dissolving (from A1.1)
background.html:
In some bonds the electrons are shared unevenly, so one end is slightly negative and the other slightly positive: the bond is polar. -OH groups are polar. Bonds between carbon and hydrogen are shared evenly: non-polar.

A hydrogen bond is a weak attraction between a slightly positive H and a slightly negative O (or N) nearby.

"Like dissolves like": water is polar, so it dissolves polar things (sugars, with many -OH groups) but not non-polar ones (oils, which are mostly C and H).

background.title: Cells, membranes and osmosis
background.html:
Every cell is surrounded by a thin membrane that controls what goes in and out. Plant cells also have a stiff cell wall outside the membrane.

Osmosis is water moving across a membrane towards the side with more dissolved substances. So if a cell fills up with dissolved sugar, water rushes in and the cell swells (an animal cell can burst). Big molecules that do not dissolve do not cause this.

background.title: Energy from food: respiration
background.html:
Cells release energy from food in respiration: glucose (or fat) is broken down with oxygen, giving carbon dioxide and water. Energy is measured in joules (J); 1 kJ = 1 000 J. "Oxidised" here means broken down with oxygen in respiration.

Building big molecules needs energy; cells get it from a small molecule called ATP, made in respiration.

background.title: Percentage change
background.html:
Percentage change = (new value − starting value) ÷ starting value × 100.

Example: 50 grows to 60. Change 10; 10 ÷ 50 = 0.2; × 100 = a 20% increase. Always divide by the value you started with (usually the earlier one).

background.title: Command terms: what the question wants
background.html:
IB questions start with a command term that tells you how much to write. The ones today (definitions from the IB Biology guide, shortened):

  • State, list, identify: a short answer, no reasons.
  • Outline: a brief account; describe: a detailed account.
  • Explain: give reasons or causes: link each feature to its effect with "SO" or "because".
  • Distinguish: make the differences clear.
  • Deduce: reach a conclusion from the information given; calculate: a number with working shown.

terms.def: A very small particle with a negative charge that moves around the centre of an atom. Bonds form when atoms share electrons.
The outermost layer of electrons around an atom. These are the electrons that take part in bonding.
A strong bond in which two atoms share a pair of electrons. Covalent bonds hold the atoms of one molecule together.
Elements that are not metals, such as hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur. They join to each other with covalent bonds.
A substance made of atoms of two or more different elements joined by bonds. Glucose (C, H and O) is a compound.
One of the small units that join in a chain to make a polymer. Glucose is the monomer of starch.
A large molecule made of many similar small units (monomers) joined in a chain. Starch, proteins and DNA are polymers.
A very large molecule, made of thousands of atoms. Polysaccharides, proteins and nucleic acids are macromolecules.
A reaction that joins two molecules with a covalent bond and releases a molecule of water. The opposite of hydrolysis.
A reaction that uses a water molecule to break a covalent bond, splitting a large molecule into smaller ones.
The covalent bond that joins two sugar units, made by condensation. "1,4" means it links carbon 1 of one sugar to carbon 4 of the next.
The covalent bond that joins two amino acids in a protein, made by condensation.
A chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. A protein is made of one or more polypeptides.
The building block of DNA and RNA: a phosphate, a sugar with five carbons and a base, joined together.
A small molecule that carries energy inside cells. Cells make it in respiration and use it to power work such as building polymers.
A protein that speeds up one particular chemical reaction in a living thing without being used up.
Breaking large food molecules into small ones in the gut, so they can be absorbed into the blood.
A single sugar unit, such as glucose or ribose: the monomer of carbohydrates.
A carbohydrate polymer: many monosaccharides joined by glycosidic bonds. Starch, glycogen and cellulose are polysaccharides.
Two monosaccharides joined by one glycosidic bond, such as maltose or sucrose.
A monosaccharide with five carbon atoms, formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>5</sub>, such as ribose.
A monosaccharide with six carbon atoms, formula C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>, such as glucose and fructose.
An oxygen atom bonded to a hydrogen atom, sticking out from a bigger molecule (a hydroxyl group). It is polar, so it forms hydrogen bonds with water.
A weak attraction between a slightly positive hydrogen atom and a slightly negative oxygen or nitrogen atom nearby, usually on another molecule.
Able to dissolve in a liquid, here water. Insoluble means it does not dissolve.
Not able to dissolve in water. Insoluble stores stay put and do not cause osmosis.
The pale yellow liquid part of blood, mostly water, in which the blood cells float.
Here: broken down with oxygen in respiration, which releases the energy stored in the molecule.
The process in every cell that releases energy from glucose or fat. With oxygen it produces carbon dioxide and water. It is not the same as breathing.
Water moving across a membrane towards the side with more dissolved substances. Osmotic means to do with osmosis.
A spiral shape, like a spring or a spiral staircase.
How strongly something resists being pulled apart. A rope has high tensile strength.
A bundle of cellulose chains held together by hydrogen bonds: the strong fibres of a plant cell wall.
A stiff layer outside the membrane of plant cells that gives the cell its shape and stops it bursting. In plants it is made of cellulose.
A very thin layer around a cell that controls what goes in and out. It is made mainly of phospholipids.
A protein with a short carbohydrate (sugar) chain attached. In membranes the chain sticks out of the cell.
A molecule, often on a cell surface, that the immune system can recognise. Foreign antigens trigger a defence.
A protein made by white blood cells that binds to one particular antigen. Antibodies can make foreign cells clump together.
The body's defence system (white blood cells and the antibodies they make) against germs and foreign cells.
Fats, oils, waxes and steroids: substances in living things that dissolve in non-polar solvents but hardly at all in water.
"Water-hating": not attracted to water, so it does not dissolve in it. Non-polar substances such as oils are hydrophobic.
"Water-loving": attracted to water, so it dissolves in or mixes with water. Polar and charged groups are hydrophilic.
Having no charged ends, because the electrons are shared evenly. Molecules made mostly of C and H are non-polar.
Having a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end, because electrons are shared unevenly. -OH groups and water are polar.
A liquid that other substances dissolve in. Water and ethanol are solvents.
A small molecule with three carbons, each carrying an -OH group. It is the backbone that fatty acids join to in fats and phospholipids.
A long chain of carbon and hydrogen atoms with an acid group (-COOH) at one end. The chain is non-polar, so it is hydrophobic.
The covalent bond formed by condensation between an -OH of glycerol and the -COOH of a fatty acid.
A small group of atoms, one phosphorus surrounded by four oxygens, with a negative charge. It makes the head of a phospholipid hydrophilic.
A fat or oil molecule: one glycerol joined by ester bonds to three fatty acids.
A lipid made of glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate group: a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails. Membranes are made of them.
A saturated fatty acid has no C=C double bonds: every carbon holds as many hydrogen atoms as it can.
An unsaturated fatty acid has at least one C=C double bond. Mono = one, poly = two or more.
The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid. Fats with a high melting point are solid at room temperature.
An animal that keeps its body warm with its own heat, whatever the outside temperature: birds and mammals.
Fat tissue: cells filled with triglyceride droplets, found under the skin and around organs.
The thick layer of adipose tissue under the skin of seals and whales.
Reducing the loss of heat. A thermal insulator is a material that heat passes through slowly.
The place where an organism lives, such as polar sea water or a warm forest.
Having a hydrophilic part and a hydrophobic part in the same molecule. A phospholipid is the main example.
A double layer. The phospholipid bilayer is two layers of phospholipids with their tails facing each other: the basis of every cell membrane.
A lipid whose molecule is four rings of carbon atoms fused together. Cholesterol, oestradiol and testosterone are steroids.
A chemical messenger made in one part of the body and carried in the blood to act on other cells (target cells).
Particles spreading from where there are many of them to where there are fewer, without the cell using energy.
A protein that a particular signal molecule fits and binds to, which then changes what the cell does.
A section of DNA that carries the instructions for one product, usually a protein.
Kilojoule: a unit of energy. 1 kJ = 1 000 joules. "kJ per gram" is the energy released by one gram.
IB command term: "give a detailed account including reasons or causes". Link each feature to its effect with SO or because.
IB command term: "give a brief account or summary". The main points only.
IB command term: "give a detailed account". What it is or what happens; reasons are not needed.
IB command term: "provide an answer from a number of possibilities". A short, specific answer.
IB command term: "make clear the differences between two or more concepts or items".
IB command term: "reach a conclusion from the information given".
IB command term: "obtain a numerical answer showing the relevant stages in the working".
IB command term: a labelled, accurate diagram in pencil, with a ruler for straight lines.
To spot and name something when you see it, here a type of molecule in a diagram.
Which way round something faces. In cellulose, each glucose faces the opposite way to its neighbour.
Joined so that neighbouring rings share a side (two atoms and the bond between them).
